title: The Leadership Discipline of Avoiding 'Just One More Thing'
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This short daily post argues that the greatest threat to a leader's priority list is not bad ideas but well-meant additions that look harmless on the surface. Each small good intention pulls attention away from the key priorities, so protecting the list takes real ruthlessness. The author offers a simple test: before taking on anything new, ask what you will remove to make space, and treat an unwillingness to drop anything as a red flag that the addition does not belong yet. He admits the discipline is hard because each new thing may genuinely be good, but the cost is watered-down focus and performance. The piece closes with the claim that leadership is about restraint, and a reading list of quotes from Karen Martin, Peter Drucker, Jim Collins and others that reinforce the case for a short priority list.
points: Well-meaning small additions are dangerous precisely because they look innocuous while eroding focus on the real priorities.
The practical test is a trade-off question: before adding anything, name what you will remove to make space for it.
If a leader is not prepared to drop anything, that unwillingness signals the new item does not fit at this stage.
Restraint, not capacity, is presented as the defining leadership discipline, because each tempting addition may be good in itself.
quotes: Never underestimate how fast good intentions can blow up the most carefully thought-out plans. They look perfectly innocuous on the surface.
The reality is that any effort which takes your focus away from your key priorities is a distraction you simply can’t afford.
To protect the momentum and clarity of the priority list, leaders have to be absolutely ruthless in protecting it. Before you take on anything new, ask what you’re going to remove to make space.
If you’re not prepared to drop anything, then that’s a big red flag; the proposed addition doesn’t fit at this stage.

The temptation to add “one more thing” is very strong, particularly when each new thing you add has the potential to be good. The danger, though, is that you end up watering down your focus and performance.
Leadership is about restraint. Keep your focus on what’s important, and good intentions will never be a source of regret the following day.
Effective executives do not make a great many decisions. They concentrate on the important ones.
